newsitem.title: UK: Firm UK retail sales pressure BoE to raise rates.
newsitem.headline: Firm UK retail sales pressure BoE to raise rates.

text.p: Strong retail sales and above trend GDP growth mean the Bank of England is even more likely to raise interest rates unless there is a significant fiscal tightening in the forthcoming budget, analysts said on Thursday.
No date has yet been set for the budget but analysts said the central bank will be keen to wait and see what finance minister Gordon Brown does to dampen down an increasingly buoyant consumer sector.
"The need for higher interest rates is clearly there. They are likely to raise rates but they'll wait and see what's in the budget," said Kevin Gardner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley
UK April retail sales rose by 0.1 percent month-on-month but by a sizeable 4.7 percent year-on-year. Over the closely watched three month period retail sales rose 1.2 percent.

Analysts said the figures confirmed the picture of an economy split two ways with a robust consumer sector and an ailing manufacturing division, dogged by the strength of the pound, which has risen 17 percent in nine months.
And figures suggested this trend was set to continue, they said.
"The three-month growth rates were strong across the board," said Adam Cole, UK economist at HSBC James Capel. "There's a real prospect of consumer spending growth increasing further this year."
Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday said he was optimistic about the state of inflation but remained concerned about the impact of the current strong economic growth.
"At the moment in the short run, it's extremely encouraging, there are very, very few inflationary pressures to be seen anywhere in the system, that's not been our concern," he said on BBC radio 4.
"What we're also seeing is robust economic growth at a rate which can't be sustained for very long without actually that giving rise to inflationary pressures further down the track," he added.
Analysts said the overwhelming message from the figures was to tighten fiscal policy by raising taxes rather than risk further stifling export competitiveness with an interest rate increase.
"Again it makes the point that the best way to tighten policy is not to raise interest rates but to raise taxes, hitting the recovery where it's strongest, on the consumer side," said Cole.
But if Brown failed to come up with a tight budget, the Bank of England would be likely to raise interest rates.

"We expect the Bank to push for a further tightening of monetary policy late in the summer, possibly earlier if chancellor (finance minister) Brown fails to deliver a tightish budget in the next few weeks," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.
Britain's next interest rate change will be the first to be decided by the Bank of England since finance minister Brown granted it operational independence.
And the Bank, noted for its preference for a tight monetary policy, warned in its inflation report this week that interest rates might have to rise again soon.
